topics: ⚖️ The Sons of Samuel — did not sin, but did not walk in their father's ways either
👑 David and Bathsheba — 'anyone who says David sinned is simply mistaken'
🗣️ David and the Slander Against Mephibosheth — a contradiction in Rav's own teachings
🏛️ Solomon's Idolatry, Reexamined — building the high places vs. failing to protest
🕊️ Josiah, the Great Penitent — or was he never really guilty at all?

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Defending David, Solomon, and Josiah
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 56a–56b
overview.hebrewSource: כׇּל הָאוֹמֵר דָּוִד חָטָא אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא טוֹעֶה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Continuing the sequence begun with Reuben, Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan defends the reputations of the sons of Samuel, King David, King Solomon, and King Josiah, reinterpreting biblical verses that seem to describe their sins. The Gemara does not let these defenses stand unchallenged: it raises real textual difficulties, cites contrary views (including from Rav himself), and works through the political and moral complexity of David's conduct toward Uriah and Mephibosheth, and Solomon's tolerance of his wives' idolatry — closing the chapter with a debate over whether Josiah was a penitent at all.

slides.title: ⚖️ Did the Sons of Samuel Really Sin?
slides.subtitle: The verse says they sought unjust gain — but what did that actually mean?
rows: They vocally demanded their tithe portions from other Levites
They imposed on homeowners to buy their merchandise
They took an extra basket of tithes by force, beyond their due
They took only what was owed them — but improperly seized it by force

callout.label: The core defense:
callout.text: 'In his ways they did not walk' — unlike their father Samuel, who traveled to judge Israel in their own towns, they stayed home to enrich their own attendants. That failure to emulate, not outright corruption, is what the verse condemns.

slides.title: 👑 'Anyone Who Says David Sinned Is Mistaken'
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani's defense meets the plain reading of Nathan's rebuke

lines.speaker: Defense
lines.text: 'David succeeded in all his ways, and the Lord was with him' — could sin have touched him while the Divine Presence remained?

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: But Nathan rebuked him: 'Why have you despised the Lord's word, to do evil?'

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: He sought to do evil but did not actually do it. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi notes: elsewhere the Torah says 'and he did' evil; here it says only 'to do' evil.

lines.speaker: On Uriah's death
lines.text: 'You killed Uriah with the sword' means: you should have judged him before the Sanhedrin for treason and did not — for Uriah called Joab 'my lord' in the king's presence.

lines.speaker: On taking Bathsheba
lines.text: 'You took his wife' means you had rights to her — soldiers going to David's wars wrote a conditional bill of divorce beforehand.

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: David's intentions were faulted, but according to this reading his actions were halakhically defensible.

slides.title: 🗣️ A Contradiction: Did David Accept Slander?
slides.subtitle: Rav's own statements seem to clash

nodes.content: ❓ Rav: examining David's whole life, no sin is found except the matter of Uriah
⚡ But Rav also said: David accepted a slanderous report (about Mephibosheth, from Ziba) — a contradiction left unresolved ('kashya')
📖 Story: Ziba slandered Mephibosheth twice; David believed him even after catching him in a lie the first time

columns.label: Rav's view
columns.content: David simply accepted the slander uncritically

columns.label: Shmuel's view
columns.content: David saw genuine corroborating evidence — Mephibosheth's disheveled appearance and bitter words

nodes.content: 💥 Consequence: when David divided the estate between them, a Divine Voice foretold that Rehoboam and Jeroboam would divide the kingdom

callout.label: Rav Yehuda cites Rav:
callout.text: Had David not accepted that report, the kingdom would not have split, Israel would not have worshipped idols, and we would not have been exiled.

slides.title: 🏛️ Solomon: Innocent Intent, or Failure to Protest?
slides.subtitle: Two proposed readings of his relationship to idolatry

boxes.title: Sought but never built
items: 'His wives turned his heart' — only an attempt, he did not follow
'He built an altar for Chemosh' — only sought to build
Rejected: the same verb describes Joshua actually building an altar, so it must mean actual construction here too

boxes.title: Accepted explanation (Rabbi Yosei)
items: Solomon did build the high places — later destroyed by Josiah
But he is blamed the way Josiah is praised: for what happened under his watch, even though earlier righteous kings share responsibility too
'He did evil' — because he should have protested his wives' idol worship and did not

callout.label: Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel:
callout.text: It would have been better for that righteous man to have served idolatry as a menial servant than for Scripture to write of him, 'he did evil in the sight of the Lord.'

slides.title: 🕊️ Josiah: Righteous From the Start, or a Penitent?
slides.subtitle: Two very different readings of the same praise

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani: 'anyone who says Josiah sinned is mistaken' — the verse calls him fully righteous from the start
2️⃣ Difficulty: 'like him there was no king who returned to the Lord' — implying repentance from actual sin
3️⃣ Resolution: every judgment he issued between ages 8 and 18 he personally repaid from his own funds, in case his youthful rulings had erred — not repentance for sin
4️⃣ Rav disagrees entirely: 'there is no greater penitent than Josiah' — and names contemporary penitents in his own generation as parallels

callout.label: Chapter's close:
callout.text: The chapter 'Bameh Behema' ends here, on this open question of how far genuine repentance, and genuine sin, extend even among the righteous.

summary.principle: The Gemara repeatedly reinterprets biblical accounts of sin among Israel's leaders — David, Solomon, Josiah — distinguishing intention from action and direct wrongdoing from a failure to protest, while leaving some contradictions candidly unresolved.

flowSteps.content: ⚖️ Sons of Samuel: did not sin outright, but failed to emulate their father's devoted judging
👑 David: sought evil but, on this reading, did not commit it; his one true lapse concerned Uriah

columns.content: 🗣️ David's acceptance of slander against Mephibosheth carried enormous consequences
🏛️ Solomon is blamed for failing to protest his wives' idolatry, not for worshipping it himself

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Scripture's harshest language can describe a failure to prevent wrongdoing, not only active sin

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's defense, what was the actual failing of the sons of Samuel?
o: They worshipped idols
They did not travel to judge Israel in their own towns as their father did, staying home instead to enrich their attendants
They stole from the Temple treasury
They refused to serve as judges at all
quiz.e: The verse 'in his ways they did not walk' is explained as their failure to emulate Samuel's practice of traveling to judge Israel in its various towns, rather than an accusation of outright corruption.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi read the phrase 'to do evil' (rather than 'and he did evil') regarding David?
o: As proof David actually sinned twice
As indicating David only sought to do evil but did not carry it out, unlike every other Torah figure described with 'and he did'
As a scribal error
As referring to a different king entirely
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi notes that every other instance of evil in the Torah is written with 'and he did,' but here it says 'to do,' suggesting David intended evil without actually performing it.

quiz.q: What contradiction does Abaye the Elder point out in Rav's statements about David?
o: Whether David was a king or a prophet
Rav says no sin is found in David's life except regarding Uriah, yet Rav also says David accepted a slanderous report about Mephibosheth
Whether David fought the Philistines or the Amalekites
Whether David wrote the Psalms
quiz.e: Abaye notes the tension between Rav's statement that David's only sin was the Uriah affair, and Rav's separate statement that David accepted lashon hara — the Gemara leaves this difficulty (kashya) unresolved.

quiz.q: According to the accepted explanation (citing Rabbi Yosei), why is Solomon blamed for building the high places of idolatry, similar to how Josiah is praised for destroying them?
o: Because he personally worshipped every idol

The verse juxtaposes them: Josiah is credited for what happened under his reign even though earlier kings did much of the work, and Solomon is blamed for what happened under his watch, since he failed to prevent it
Because Solomon lived longer than Josiah
Because the verses are unrelated
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that just as Josiah is credited with destroying idols largely removed by his predecessors, Solomon is blamed for the high places built under his reign because he failed to protest, even if he did not personally worship there.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara reinterpret the verse that 'there was no king like Josiah who returned to the Lord,' given the claim that Josiah never actually sinned?
o: It refers to Josiah's mother's repentance, not his own
It refers to his repaying, from his own money, every judgment he issued between the ages of 8 and 18, in case his youthful rulings had erred — not repentance from actual sin
It is simply rejected as inauthentic
It refers to Josiah's decision to rebuild the Temple
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that Josiah personally reimbursed parties from cases he judged as a child (ages 8-18) out of concern he may have judged incorrectly, and this act of returning money is what the verse calls 'returning to the Lord,' not repentance for sin.
